text: Good evening. Welcome everyone to the April 8th, 2026 meeting of the audit committee. Thank you for being here. Hope everyone had a good break. My name is Anne Donahue. I am the chair of the committee. With me are my fellow committee members, Mr. John Pepper and Ms. Amy Riccardi. As a reminder, this meeting is being audio recorded. It is not being live streamed, and it is not being video recorded, but it is being audio recorded and will be available to listen to in the future through the LCPS website.

The second item on our agenda is public comment. But as we do not have any individuals signed up for public comment, we will move on to item number three, which is review of the minutes from our March 4th, 2026 meeting. The draft minutes have been posted on BoardDocs, and we have a hard copy here in front of us. Hopefully, we've all had a chance to review the drafts. If any of my colleagues have any requests or suggestions for

edits or changes, now is the opportunity to do so. And if there are no edits or changes, I will entertain a motion to approve the minutes. So moved. Thank you, Ms. Riccardi. Is there a second? Second. The motion has been properly moved and seconded. Is there any discussion? Seeing no discussion, all those in favor, please raise your hand and say aye. Aye. Aye. Aye. That motion passes unanimously. And now we will move on to item number four, our discussion item,

Officer of the Auditor General's program timeline. Mr. Woods, the floor is yours. Thank you, Madam Chair. And this timeline is intended to provide the committee with a clear high-level view of major audit milestones and scheduled touchpoints throughout the calendar year, including when items will come to this committee for discussion,

information, or action, and when certain items will advance to the school board. As outlined in the timeline, today's meeting includes the program timeline discussion and the risk assessment overview as information. The audit universe is scheduled to be presented at our next meeting in May as an information item. Quarterly updates are planned throughout the year to keep the committee informed to audit progress. In August,

we plan to present the audit plan and audit universe to come forward as an audit committee action plan. This action plan will give the committee its first time to approve an annual audit plan, so we do look forward to that in August. Followed us presenting that audit plan here to the committee, we will then provide the school board with this information as an information item or a work session.

We do not determine, or I do not determine the agenda item, so sometimes we do try to put on the work session, but because the school board agenda can get kind of busy, it may be moved to an information item to be presented later in the evening during a school board meeting. The timeline concludes with the 2026 annual report. The annual report is provided annually to the committee and to the board and is a capture of the

prior year work done of the Auditor General. Once we present it to the committee, it will subsequently be discussed to the school board. The timeline also notes, if needed, special audit committee meetings may be scheduled in response to significant audit findings or emerging issues. And so as those arise, we may need to schedule a meeting or add it to our agenda

when necessary. Overall, this document is designed to reinforce predictability, transparency, and shared expectations around the OAG's annual planning and reporting cycle. There is no action requested today or in the future of this item. I'm happy to answer any questions or receive any feedback on the timeline that you all may have. Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Woods. Mr. Pepper?

it was a priority to internal audit, which is the OIG office. And so there is a discussion amongst us in the committee, which audits are priority and which audits should be prioritized. Ricardi's question and your statement, how you go about prioritizing your recommendations for the audit universe? So if it's based on the survey, it's occurrence of items that are brought up from principals, senior staff, school board. Also, if an event occurs, it may have a low frequency of occurring, but if the impact is high,

then that identified risk would move up, as opposed to something that may occur frequently on these surveys or in a review, but the impact to the school and to students is low. And so that will be a lower risk item. Also, if there are new topical items. Topical item or topical requirements are

items that the Institute of Internal Audit has determined we should focus on. It could be performing a risk review, it could be performing a review or performing an audit, but they do require us to at least look into it as a risk assessment option. And so, to go back to your question, it's several things to identify

the audit universe. And those topical requirements, we will put in the universe because they are a standard that we now have incorporated. And so if we decide to do them, great this year. But if we need to do them next year, then they'll go on the following year, and they'll stay on the universe every year until we perform them. And so it's several ways we identify the audit topics.

Thank you for that, Mr. Woods. And you indicated that you get ideas for what to potentially include in the audit universe from a number of sources. so you said, is the IIA the one that you said that has the guidelines so far? And then do you localize them for LCPS or customize them or contextualize them for LCPS? Yes. Okay, great. Yeah. And I'm assuming that's weighing risk management issues, financial risk management, safety, security, and whatever else is on that list, but it'd be really great to see that. Yes. And I'm glad you brought that up. When I provide a survey, so a survey will be administered to school board members.

In that survey administered to school board members, I will identify what the topical requirements are. One of them we've already done, which is third-party risk management. Another one would be cybersecurity. Those are the two I can think of off the top of my head right now,

but I will identify all of them when we are performing the survey, and so you will have that information at that time. Great. Thank you. Mm-hmm. Thank you, Mr. Woods. Thanks. We don't have any other questions on that topic right now. We can move on to item number 5.01, your fiscal year '27 risk assessment. Thank you.

The risk assessment is a core component of internal audit planning and serves as a foundation for developing a risk-based annual audit plan. As outlined in the attachment, this process is not intended to be a checklist, but rather a strategic tool used to evaluate risks that could affect the division's ability to achieve its objectives, comply with requirements, safeguard assets, and operate effectively. For fiscal year '27, the Office of the Auditor General, or the OAG, will gather

and evaluate risk information from a multiple number of areas. Risk surveys will be administered to school board members, senior leadership, and principals. We will review prior internal and applicable external audit recommendations. We will evaluate documentation, reporting, and compliance requirements. We will also analyze the organization's objectives, strategies, and operating environment. We are currently going through a new

strategic plan, so we will use draft language from that plan to incorporate into our review of risk assessment. We will also consider governance-related factors such as oversight, delegation, and accountability. Give you a second just to take a look at the attachment. Next slide, please. Once collected, risks will be evaluated and prioritized

and used to update the audit universe, and ultimately incorporated into a proposed risk-based annual audit plan. That proposed plan will later be presented to the audit committee, as we previously discussed, for review, input, and approval. Today's item is to provide the committee with visibility into the process and sequence of events of the OAG's risk assessment process. At this time, I welcome any questions regarding this process.
None at this time. Please continue. Final agenda item. Sorry, Mr. Woods. I didn't realize we were

complete with that item. I don't think we have any questions at this time, so we can move on to your information item 5.02, the Office of the Auditor General newsletter. Yes. The final item I'm presenting today is the OAG newsletter. The OAG is in the early stages of developing a periodic newsletter intended to improve communication and awareness of our work across the division. This includes the audit committee, the school board, and division staff.

The newsletter is envisioned as a brief, concise publication that may include updates on ongoing or recently completed audits, highlights of common themes or lessons learned, information about audit-related resources or best practices. So topical requirements, if they ever come up as recommended audits, we'll throw those in there as well, so the community will understand why those items ended up on the audit

universe or in our audit plan. And general updates related to internal audit and accountability.The newsletter has yet to be issued. Today's item is simply an early awareness update to let the committee know that this initiative is underway and to explain its purpose and anticipated structure. There is no action requested on this matter now or in the future.

As we continue to develop the newsletter, the OAG will be mindful of clarity and consistency in alignment with LCPS expectations. I'm happy to answer any questions or receive feedback for the newsletter at this time. Thank you, Mr. Woods. I applaud the proposal. I think this is a great idea. I understand that it's still in a development phase, but I wondered if you had any thoughts at this time of what you're

anticipating as far as frequency and who the newsletter would be going out to. What kind of content do you think you're looking to have? So we plan to issue the newsletter quarterly. We're trying to figure out the logistics of how we will issue the newsletter. Do we want to attach it to the superintendent's newsletter, or do we want to send it separately?

The obstacles of sending it separately is, are we putting too much information to the community from our division if we don't attach it to something that already has a cadence to how we issue something. And so, we do know how often, quarterly, we're just trying to figure out what is the best way and manner to issue the newsletter. For principals, it could be attached to a principal update,

which they perform weekly. So somewhere in a quarter, we can attach it to a public or a principal update. But for the public and the greater community, it's just determining what is the best way to provide that information without overloading them with information they already receive from their child in ParentVUE or through the superintendent's office or other publications that come out of LCPS.

Again, I think this is a great idea. I'm looking forward to it. A couple of follow-up questions. I would imagine that any newsletter would include contact information for your office to provide feedback or follow-up for the community. Do you anticipate ever conducting polls or specifically asking for community feedback on various topics?

Currently, that's not in the works. I recall a meeting with the local auditors in Oregon who actually poll their local community for audit topics as well, and that they include in their audit universe that they present to the audit committee. I don't know if we want to go to that level, but now that you bring it up, if the community would like us to poll the community,

we certainly can do that in the future if we think that's a best practice. Thank you for that. And as a parent of two students who attend separate LCPS elementary schools, I appreciate that you're sensitive to the amount of communication that goes out to the community and the possibility of becoming overwhelmed or missing things. Yes. And we have two individuals. One has a student in our office, one has a student

currently in elementary, another has two who have matriculated through LCPS. And so, it helps rely on them to understand what communications they receive as a parent. Also, we rely greatly on communications, DCE, is it Family Communications Department? For helping us in how we communicate to the public. Thank you. Sorry. Ms. Record.

Thank you. Yeah, I'm really excited about this too. I think it's a really great opportunity for your office to share. I think people have heard the phrase, in some cases, what an auditor general is, but they don't have any idea what you do. So I think it'll be a really great way for you to communicate that at least out to the public. I think one of the things I always get concerned about and that I work with my clients on when they're doing surveys or they're going out to the community is if you're going to ask, then there's got to be some

action on the back end. And I don't know, bandwidth-wise, whether or not you all have the bandwidth yet to be able to take action. It's great to get the feedback- Mm-hmm ... for sure, but I think you've also got to measure. We're already going to get, I'm sure, a pretty substantial laundry list of items. And when you go out to the community to ask for more, it's just going to make it even bigger. It's a pro and con thing. I don't know that I have necessarily a set viewpoint on that, but I always like

to say, if you're going to survey and you're going to ask people, then you better be ready to take the action on it. So I think we just have to level set the expectation about receiving the input, but not necessarily being able to deliver the output on that quantity of potential input you might be getting. So I think it's just something to be mindful of as we're doing it. I think it might be interesting to maybe even do that in a phased approach where you're starting with a smaller audience of, you said principals- Yes

... and administrators and board. Yes. And see what you get from that first, and then maybe in another year then expand that out to the public at some point. I don't know. I'm just throwing out ideas at this point in time because I think you ask this community, you're going to get an awful lot, and the question then becomes, you don't want them to really say, "Well, he asked," but they didn't do anything with it. Right? Correct. And it goes about, well, who is prioritized in that?

Because usually the voices we'll hear the most are those who are unhappiest. The happiest voices are usually going about their business. And so when those voices do respond, and it doesn't end up on our docket to perform an audit, they'll become disillusioned, and so it becomes one of what you said. Once we take those responses, and it doesn't end up, it looks like we're not doing anything about it.

Also, the principals are 100, give or take, and so their responses alone are a lot. And so when you do add the community in, it does become a lot. We do have a hotline currently, and that is open to the public. And any time the public wants to submit a hotline concern, it is available. And so there is an avenue for them to reach us, and submit a concern that doesn't necessarily have to end up

in the audit universe. But because of their concerns, some of the things that they do indirectly do end up on the audit universe. And so I won't go in deep detail, but the universes we have provided in the past, some of the items have been a result of information submitted on the hotline from community members. Great. I think that's great. And it's not that I don't want to hear from the community, because absolutely I do.

It's just I'm worried about the bandwidth- Yeah ... and capacity issue, and then also the responsiveness- Yeah ... question too. So it's just all part of the stuff in the mix that you've got to sort out as you're building this out. But I'm excited for the newsletter. I think it's going to be great, and I think, even a kind of a phased approach with the public in explaining and rolling out what you do, and I think sharing the hotline again and what the purpose of that is, I think is really important. So thank you for doing this. Thank you. Mr. Pepper.
